title: The Jesus Piece
description:
13 Oct 2026 · @Elisha Babalola

The greatest obstacle to truth may not be ignorance itself, but the conviction that we already possess the truth.
content:
If he came today
If Jesus walked into a city today, I doubt most of us would follow him. I don't mean the cynics. I mean the people most sure they already know God.
Two thousand years ago, the people who missed him weren't short on knowledge. They had more of it than anyone. The Pharisees didn't miss Jesus because they knew too little. They missed him because they were sure they knew enough.
That is the argument of this piece. The greatest obstacle to truth may not be ignorance itself, but the conviction that we already possess the truth. And a society that loses the ability to question its own convictions slowly loses the ability to change.
The unlikely followers
Look at who followed him first. Fishermen. A tax collector. Women whose word a court of the time would not accept. The book of Acts calls Peter and John "unschooled, ordinary men" (Acts 4:13).
Jesus seemed to expect this. "You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children" (Matthew 11:25). Paul later reminded the church in Corinth that "not many of you were wise by human standards" (1 Corinthians 1:26-27).
Now look at who resisted. It was the chief priests and the Pharisees, the people trusted to guard the truth, who met to plan his death (John 11:47-53).
And on the morning of the resurrection, the first witnesses were women (John 20). The historian Josephus records that a woman's testimony was not accepted in court at the time (Antiquities 4.219). The message was trusted first to the people society trusted least.
Not ignorance, but openness
It is tempting to say the first followers had one great quality: ignorance. I used to put it that way. But it is the wrong word, and the story itself shows why.
The disciples were observant Jews who knew their scriptures. Paul was a trained Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea sat among the leaders, and Gamaliel, one of the most respected teachers of the day, argued for patience over persecution (Acts 5:34-39).
So the line was never between people who knew things and people who didn't. It was between people who held their knowledge loosely and people for whom knowledge had become identity and power.
What the first followers had was not ignorance but openness: a mind still willing to be surprised. Socrates called it knowing that you do not know. Today we would call it intellectual humility.
The trap of certainty
Certainty feels like strength, but it works like a locked door. Once we are sure, new evidence stops being information and starts being a threat.
The historian Daniel Boorstin put it well: "The greatest obstacle to discovery is not ignorance, it is the illusion of knowledge" (Quote Investigator). The religious leaders were not stupid. They were invested, and their status, income and sense of who they were rested on the answer they already had.
So I would name the real failure differently. Not ignorance, but three habits that look like knowledge:
1. Handing our thinking to an authority we never question.
2. Conforming because everyone around us does.
3. Refusing to look at what we would rather not see.
Everyone outsources
The first of those habits has a problem, and it is worth facing honestly. The disciples also handed their thinking to someone else. They followed Jesus.
In truth, everyone outsources most of what they believe. I trust doctors, maps and engineers I will never meet. The philosopher John Hardwig called this epistemic dependence, and Steven Sloman and Philip Fernbach's The Knowledge Illusion shows how much of what we "know" actually lives in other people's heads.
So the question is not whether we trust, but how. Healthy trust updates when the evidence changes. Unhealthy trust cannot, because changing it would cost us our place in the group.
Openness cuts both ways
Openness is not a virtue on its own. The same willingness to follow something new also led crowds after Theudas and Judas the Galilean, two movements that collapsed. Gamaliel used them as his warning (Acts 5:36-37).
A mind that believes anything is as stuck as a mind that believes nothing new. The cognitive scientist Hugo Mercier argues in Not Born Yesterday that people are, on the whole, careful about whom they believe, and should be.
What matters is not being easy to persuade. It is being persuadable by the right things: evidence, consistency, and what a teaching produces over time.
When institutions protect themselves from the truth
Every institution starts as a way to protect something true. A temple keeps a faith alive, a university preserves knowledge, a medical body keeps patients safe. The danger begins when the institution starts protecting itself from the truth instead.
History repeats the pattern. In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that doctors who washed their hands saved mothers' lives, and the medical establishment mocked him. The Catholic Church condemned Galileo in 1633 and formally acknowledged its error in 1992.
Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions shows the same resistance inside science: fields defend their framework until a new generation replaces it. Upton Sinclair gave the reason: "It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends on his not understanding it."
Jesus did not reject the institution itself. "I have not come to abolish the Law... but to fulfil" (Matthew 5:17). His charge was sharper: "You nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition" (Mark 7:13).
Societies that cannot question themselves
This is where the argument leaves the first century. A society needs the capacity to question itself: to notice when its traditions are failing, when its leaders are dishonest, and when its beliefs about the world need to change.
The evidence for that is strong. Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics for showing that societies with open, accountable institutions grow richer. Joel Mokyr shared the 2025 prize, and his book A Culture of Growth argues that Europe took off when challenging inherited authority became normal.
Karl Popper made the philosophical case decades earlier in The Open Society and Its Enemies. A society that cannot criticise its own ideas cannot correct them.
In many struggling societies, including my own, I see the opposite. Ideas, cultures and religious authorities are held so tightly that their flaws cannot be named, even when every sign points to them. Responsibility is handed to a pastor, an imam, a tradition or a deity instead of being examined.
But the easy version of this claim is wrong, and I want to be careful with it. Religion does matter more to people in poorer countries (Pew, 2020). Yet Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart argue the arrow mostly runs the other way: insecurity drives religiosity, not the reverse (Sacred and Secular).
The United States is both rich and deeply religious (Pew, 2019). Joseph Henrich's The Secret of Our Success shows that traditions often carry real wisdom no one can fully explain.
And dogma does not need a god. The officially atheist Soviet Union forced its scientists to deny modern genetics for years. The problem is not religion. It is any belief a society is no longer allowed to question.
The question that stays
The first followers weren't ignorant. They were unattached. They could still be surprised.
If Jesus came today, I suspect he would again be recognised first by the people with the least to lose from being wrong. That should leave every one of us, believers included, with an uncomfortable question: what truth would I miss because I am already sure?
Institutions are built to protect the truth. People, churches and nations begin to fail when they start protecting themselves from it.
Sources

title: Why the sky is blue (and sunsets are red)
description: Chatting about random subject, that I studied about
content:
You asked why the sky is blue at noon and red at sunset. It's really just a mixture of geometry, scattering (Rayleigh scattering), and, as I like to say, light diffusion. LOL.

At noon, sunlight travels through a relatively shorter distance in the atmosphere because the Sun is high in the sky (upwards closer to 90 degrees). Sunlight, consists of different colours of visible light, commonly represented by ROYGBIV, ranging from red, with longer wavelengths and lower frequencies, to violet, with shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies.

Now, here's where things get interesting. Earth's atmosphere contains tiny particles as tiny as some of the visible lights wavelength, particularly molecules of gases, that interact with sunlight. These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light much more strongly than longer wavelengths. This phenomenon is called Rayleigh scattering.

Blue and violet light have shorter wavelengths, so they are scattered more strongly in different directions as sunlight passes through the atmosphere. When we look up at the sky, some of this scattered light reaches our eyes, and we perceive the sky as blue. That's where my idea of light diffusion comes in. Although, to be scientifically precise, the process we're describing here is scattering, not diffusion.

Now, let's take a journey towards sunset.

As the Sun appears lower in the sky, sunlight has to travel through a much longer path in the atmosphere before reaching us. Think of it as the difference between taking a shortcut and taking the longest route possible. The lower the Sun gets towards the horizon, the more atmosphere its light generally has to pass through.

This longer journey means that more of the blue and violet light is scattered out of the direct beam of sunlight before it reaches our eyes. As a result, the light that comes directly from the Sun becomes richer in the longer wavelengths, particularly red, orange and yellow. That's why we sometimes see a yellow, orange or deep red Sun at sunset.

Meanwhile, the atmosphere continues to scatter blue light in different directions, so the sky can still appear blue in other parts of the atmosphere, although the colors and their intensity depend on atmospheric conditions.

And that's essentially it: the sky appears blue because atmospheric molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of sunlight more strongly, while sunsets appear red or orange because sunlight travels through more atmosphere, removing more of those shorter wavelengths from the direct beam.

Physics is beautiful, isn't it?

title: When Analogies Become Evidence
description: For some time now, I've felt conflicted about analogies, especially how often they're used in our sermons. Using analogies isn't the problem. They're great tools that make teachings and ideas easier to grasp. My problem starts when they're used as evidence. A well-told story can make an argument feel true without showing that it is true. Because we naturally think in stories, it can quietly skip the real question: does this actually follow? An analogy shows that two things are similar. Take the analogies away from many religious claims and arguments, and many would struggle to stand. Faith doesn't require switching off critical thinking. Taking God seriously should make us more careful about what's actually true.
content:
Analogies are powerful.

They help us understand complicated ideas by connecting them to things we already know. A preacher can take an abstract theological concept and explain it through farming, relationships, money, family, business, warfare, or everyday Nigerian life. When done well, an analogy can make a difficult idea suddenly clear.

The problem starts when the analogy stops being an illustration and starts being treated as evidence.

This happens often in Christian preaching. A preacher tells a story about a farmer planting seeds, a businessman making an investment, or a father providing for his children. The story is compelling, and the conclusion sounds reasonable. But a compelling story is not necessarily evidence.

Consider this claim:

“A farmer who plants more seeds can expect a greater harvest. Therefore, the more money you give to God, the more financial blessings you will receive.”

This moves from an observation about farming to a conclusion about theology and money. The farming image illustrates the idea of sowing and reaping. By itself, however, it does not establish everything the preacher has concluded from it.

A preacher might respond that this isn't merely his analogy; Paul himself uses the language of sowing and reaping. In 2 Corinthians 9:6, Paul writes that whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. That is a fair point, and it deserves a fair answer.

But context matters.

Paul was discussing generosity, specifically in the context of a collection for believers in Jerusalem. Later in the passage, he describes God as supplying and multiplying what is needed so that believers can continue being generous. The passage certainly connects generosity with God's provision and blessing, but that is different from establishing a guaranteed financial return on every monetary gift.

The question, therefore, is not simply **“Did Paul use the analogy?”**

The better question is:

“What was Paul using the analogy to communicate?”

That distinction is important because even a biblical analogy does not automatically justify every conclusion someone draws from it. We still have to examine what the text actually says, the context in which it was written, and whether the conclusion being preached follows from it.

That is the central distinction:

An analogy demonstrates similarity; evidence supports a claim.

Those are not the same thing.

An analogy can make an argument *feel* true without actually establishing that it is true. Humans naturally understand the world through stories, comparisons, and patterns. Because of this, a powerful analogy can sometimes bypass a more important question:

Does this actually follow?

This becomes especially important when the claims are about God.

Someone might say:

“A good earthly father wants his children to have good things. God is our Father. Therefore, God wants every Christian to be wealthy.”

The analogy between an earthly father and God has genuine theological value. Scripture itself uses fatherhood to communicate something about God's relationship with His people. But the conclusion that every Christian should therefore be wealthy requires additional justification.

The analogy alone cannot carry that weight.

None of this means analogies are bad. Quite the opposite.

Jesus frequently used parables, metaphors, and everyday images to communicate profound ideas: seeds, shepherds, lamps, coins, houses, servants, and weddings.

The problem isn't **using analogies**.

The problem is **confusing an analogy with evidence**.

It helps to distinguish three levels:

An analogy **illustrates** an idea when it makes an established point easier to understand.
It supports an idea when there is independent reason to believe that the comparison holds in the specific way being argued.
It proves an idea only when the evidence actually establishes the conclusion. An analogy, by itself, rarely does this.

Many sermon analogies belong to the first category but are presented as though they belong to the third.

When listening to a sermon, it is worth asking a few questions:

What exactly is the claim being made?

What is the evidence for it?

Is the preacher interpreting a biblical text, or attaching a biblical story to an idea he already holds?

What does the passage actually say in context?

Does the conclusion follow from the evidence?

And perhaps most importantly:

If I remove the story or analogy, does the argument still stand?

If removing the analogy causes the argument to collapse, then the analogy may be doing the work that evidence was supposed to do.

Faith does not require abandoning critical thinking. Asking whether an argument actually follows from its evidence is not necessarily a lack of faith. If anything, taking claims about God seriously should make us more careful about distinguishing between:

* what Scripture says,
* what can reasonably be inferred from Scripture,
* what someone personally experienced, and
* what simply makes for a powerful sermon.

A beautiful analogy can illuminate an idea.

A moving testimony can inspire someone.

A compelling story can change how someone thinks.

But none of these should automatically be mistaken for proof.

The moment an analogy is treated as evidence, we stop asking whether the conclusion is actually true and start accepting it because the story made it feel true.

That is where a useful teaching device can become a dangerous way of reasoning.
